It is a settled principle of law that the prosecution has to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt and for this the prosecution has to stand on its own legs.
IDENTITY OF THE ACCUSED AND THE OFFENDING VEHICLE.

16. The prosecution has alleged that the accused, while operating a WagonR car with registration number DL-5CJ-9941, did so under the influence of alcohol on a public roadway in a reckless and negligent manner.
This resulted in damage or loss to the rear portion of the complainant's vehicle.
To substantiate its case, the prosecution presented the complainant, referred to as PW-1, as its primary witness.
PW-1 corroborated the prosecution's account by providing a detailed statement.
According to PW-1, on March 17, 2022, at approximately 1:30 am, he and his companions were en route to Old Rajender Nagar in a Hyundai i20 vehicle registered as DL-8CAA-4447.

As the vehicle reached Rani Jhansi Road near a Honda Showroom, a silver WagonR car with the registration number DL-5CJ-9941 suddenly approached from behind in a reckless and negligent manner,
colliding with the rear section of his car, resulting in damage.
The complainant was also able to correctly identify the accused during the court proceedings.

17. Additionally, two other witnesses, namely PW-2 Ct. Manoj Kumar and PW-5 ASI Chander Pal,
testified that they arrived at the scene in response to DD No. 11 A Ex. PW-5/A and observed both the offending vehicle with registration number DL-5CJ- 9941 and the victim's vehicle with registration number DL- 8CAA-4447 in an accident-damaged condition.

They also PS- Paharganj State Vs.

21. In order to constitute an offence punishable under Section 279 IPC, the following ingredients must be made out:-
i) there must be rash or negligent driving or riding;
ii) it must be on a public way; &
iii) the driving or riding must be in a manner so rash or negligent so as to endanger human life or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any person other than the driver.

22. For appreciating the scope of the provisions aforesaid, following may be taken note of: In Rathnashalvan v. State of Karnataka reported as (2007) 3 SCC 474, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has elaborated on the law surrounding cases of rash and negligent acts and distinguished between 'rashness' and 'negligence' in the following term- State vs Surender Singh on 18 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135723944/

sentences.text: Culpable negligence lies in the failure to exercise reasonable and proper care and the extent of its reasonableness will always depend upon the circumstances of each case.
Rashness means doing an act with the PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 9/22  consciousness of a risk that evil consequences will follow but with the hope that it will not.

sentences.text: Negligence is a breach of duty imposed by law.
In criminal cases, the amount and degree of negligence are determining factors.

A question whether the accused's conduct amounted to culpable rashness or negligence depends directly on the question as to what is the amount of care and circumspection which a prudent and reasonable man would consider it to be sufficient considering all the circumstances of the case.

Criminal rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is dangerous or wanton and the further knowledge that it may cause injury but done without any intention to cause injury or knowledge that it would probably be caused.
8. As noted above, rashness consists in hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is so, and that it may cause injury.
The criminality lies in such a case in running the risk of doing such an act with recklessness or indifference as to the consequences.

Criminal negligence on the other hand, is the gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 10/22 proper care and precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which, having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge has arisen it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted.

9. The distinction has been very aptly pointed out by Holloway J. in these words:
"Culpable rashness is acting with the consciousness that the mischievous and illegal consequences may follow, but with accused was driving a vehicle WagonR car bearing registration No. DL-5CJ-9941 (shall be referred to as offending vehicle), under influence of liquor, on a public way, in rash and negligent manner so as to endanger human life and personal safety of others, which resulted in damage/ loss of the back part of vehicle of complainant the hope that they will not, and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The immutability arises from acting despite the consciousness (luxuria).

Culpable negligence is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 11/22 him, and State vs Surender Singh on 18 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135723944/
6

The imputability arises from the neglect of the civic duty of circumspection."

Mad HCR pp. 119- 20.)"

23. From the exposition of law outlined hereinabove, it is apparent that to establish the offence under Section 279 IPC, the 'commission of a rash or negligent act' has to be proved, apart of course from proving the presence of the accused at the spot driving the offending vehicle in question.

That is to say, the onus is on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused engaged himself in the commission of an act which could be called 'rash' or 'negligent'.
24.

The complainant, presented as the victim and the sole eyewitness for the prosecution, testified that on March 17, 2022, around 1:30 am, he and his friends were driving to Old Rajender Nagar after having dinner at Bara Hindu Rao.
They were in a Hyundai i20 car bearing no. DL-8CAA-4447.

Upon reaching Rani Jhansi Road near the Honda Showroom, a silver WagonR car with the license plate DL-5CJ-9941 suddenly approached from behind in a reckless and negligent manner, colliding with the rear of his car and causing damage.
Subsequently, he dialed the emergency number 100.

Police officers arrived at the scene, took both the complainant and the accused to the police station,
and seized both vehicles.
The witness emphasized that the accused appeared to be heavily intoxicated at the time of the incident.
PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 12/22 25
. As per the complainant's testimony, the accused, operating the offending vehicle, while under the influence of alcohol, was driving on a public road in a reckless and negligent manner.
In the process, the accused collided with the rear portion of the complainant's vehicle, resulting in damage to the latter.

However, during his cross-examination conducted by the learned counsel representing the accused, PW-1 (the complainant) conceded that he was unable to determine the speed of the offending vehicle at the moment of impact, given that it was positioned behind his own vehicle.
This admission by the witness contradicts his earlier assertion that the accused was driving recklessly and negligently when the accident occurred.
It is significant because if the complainant could not gauge the speed of the offending vehicle, he lacked the basis to make an objective assessment of how it was being driven.
This particular admission by the witness undermines the very foundation upon which the prosecution's case relies.

26. In light of this contradiction, it becomes imperative to scrutinize the reliability of the complainant's account, as it raises doubts about the accuracy of his initial claim regarding the accused's manner of driving.
Consequently, this admission introduces an element of uncertainty into the prosecution's case and challenges its core allegations.

Progressing further, as noted above, there exists a conspicuous absence of evidence demonstrating that the vehicle was being driven in a hazardous or reckless fashion, with knowledge that such conduct was highly likely to result in injury to individuals or damage to other vehicles traversing the PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 13/22 roadways.

sentences.text: There is no evidence to support the contention that the vehicle was being driven at high speed or in an erratic manner.
It is noteworthy that only one solitary eyewitness, namely the complainant/victim, surfaces in this matter.
It must be underscored that the complainant himself has not sustained any bodily harm as a consequence of the alleged incident.
The complainant alleges that the back side of his vehicle suffered damage due to the collision with the accused's vehicle.
Conversely, the accused maintains that the accident was occasioned by the complainant's act of sudden applying of brake.

In light of these circumstances and the absence of any independent corroboration of the complainant's assertions, one cannot entirely discount the prospect of a false imputation, particularly given the complainant's vested interest as a witness in the present circumstances.
It is apparent that in order to ascribe criminal liability to the accused, the prosecution bears the onus of proving his reckless conduct and failure to exercise due care.
Regrettably, the prosecution's case falls woefully short of establishing that the accused operated the impugned vehicle in a manner evincing a blatant disregard for the lives and safety of others.

28. Furthermore, it is pertinent to highlight that PW-1, the complainant, has testified that at the time of the incident in question, he was accompanied by his friends who were en route to Old Rajender Nagar, with the purpose of dropping them off after having dinner at Bara Hindu Rao.
Notably, none of these friends has been included in the investigation of this case to corroborate the prosecution's version of events.
No reasonable PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 14/22 explanation has been offered to account for their absence in the investigation process.

sentences.text: The conspicuous absence of independent witnesses casts doubt upon the veracity and reliability of the complainant's narrative.
In the absence of corroborating testimony from individuals who were purportedly present at the scene, the prosecution's case becomes susceptible to questions regarding its accuracy and completeness.
This raises concerns about the overall strength and credibility of the prosecution's account of the events in question.

29. Keeping in view the attending circumstances, as discussed above, it may be safely concluded that the prosecution has failed to show a genuine effort to make any independent public witness with regards the accused having caused the accident, particularly in view of the fact that it's the defence of the accused that no accident as alleged was caused by him and further that the complainant was himself driving the vehicle rashly and negligently and suddenly applied brakes due to which accident occurred.
30. Further, the failure to conduct spot photography is another glaring lapse in the investigation process.
Spot photography serves as crucial visual evidence, documenting the crime scene and aiding in the understanding of the sequence of events.
It assists in establishing the condition of the vehicles involved, the positioning of the vehicles, and any other relevant physical evidence.
The absence of spot photography raises concerns about the thoroughness and integrity of the investigation, thereby weakening the prosecution's case.

In the absence of suitable crime scene photography, the court is left bereft of a visual record PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page State vs Surender Singh on 18 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135723944/
8 15/22 to rely upon.

sentences.text: This omission is particularly significant in cases of road accidents, where the precise positioning of vehicles, skid marks, and other physical evidence can contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the incident.
The lack of photographic evidence compromises the court's ability to objectively assess the circumstances and make an informed judgment.
Undoubtedly, this lapse diminishes the strength and substance of the prosecution's case.

Moreover,
it is imperative to note that the mechanical inspection reports pertaining to the vehicles implicated in the purported incident, merely produce a concise account of the damages sustained by the said vehicles, without delving into the underlying factors that may have caused such damages.

The same are not significantly conclusive in determining the guilt of the accused U/s 279 IPC.
31.
Moreover, there exist significant and material contradictions within the prosecution's case that cast doubt upon the integrity of the investigative process.

It is crucial to note that, during cross-examination, PW-1, the complainant, affirmed that the police presence at the scene lasted a mere five minutes, after which both he and the accused, along with their vehicles, were promptly taken to the police station.
Additionally, PW-1 acknowledged submitting his complaint, marked as Ex. PW1/A, at the police station.

However, in stark contrast to this account, during cross-examination, PW-5, the Investigating Officer (IO), firmly asserted that the complainant's statement was recorded at the scene at approximately 2:30 am.
Furthermore, the IO's deposition revealed that the accused was arrested on the spot around 6:30 am on the same day.

These discrepancies stand in PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 16/22 direct contradiction to the assertions made by PW-1, the complainant, and lend credence to the suspicion that the entirety of the investigation was conducted within the confines of the police station.

sentences.text: This situation impairs the credibility and raises questions about the fairness and transparency of the investigative process as a whole.

32. Further, PW2/ Ct. Manoj Kumar and PW5/ASI Chander Pal provided testimonies narrating the prosecution's case, affirming their arrival at the accident scene after receiving information about the incident on the relevant date.
These witnesses attested to observing both the offending vehicle and the accused at the scene.
They also detailed the procedural aspects, including the recording of the FIR and the subsequent submission of the rukka.
It is however noted that none of these witnesses, in midst of performing these procedural steps, deposed as to examining the skid marks on the spot of the accident.
The same could have been used to establish the speed/the manner in which the offending vehicle caused the accident.
But not to be.
Such lapses on part of the IO in vehicular accident cases leave a yawning gap qua proving the case in a court of law, exactly what has happened in the instant case at hand as well.
Even the site plan filed on record, does not show the respective positioning of the vehicles at the time of alleged incident.
It also fails to specify the exact place of incident as the 'Mark A' as referred as the place of accident, is missing in the site plan.

As such,
therefore, the same are found to be not entirely reliable.
33. As observed above, there is no independent witness to support the case of the prosecution.
Independent witnesses PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 17/22 provide an unbiased perspective and can corroborate or challenge the testimonies of the involved parties.

sentences.text:
In the present case, the absence of independent witnesses creates a void in the evidentiary landscape, leaving the court with no reliable means to corroborate either the accused's or the complainant's version of State vs Surender Singh on 18 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135723944/
9 events.
The conflicting narratives put forth by both the accused and the complainant further exacerbate the situation.
Both parties accuse each other of negligence, which necessitates a thorough examination of the evidence and an assessment of the credibility of their claims.
In the absence of concrete evidence and reliable witnesses, it becomes arduous to ascertain the actual cause of the accident and apportion blame solely on the accused.
In light of the foregoing, it is incumbent upon the court to ensure that the prosecution discharges its burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
In the present case, the prosecution has failed to provide substantial evidence to establish the guilt of the accused.

The absence of public witnesses, the failure to conduct spot photography, the lack of suitable crime scene documentation, and the absence of independent witnesses all combine to create reasonable doubt.

Therefore, in adherence to established legal principles and precedents, so far as the allegation u/s 279 IPC is concerned, this court finds that the prosecution has failed to discharge its burden of proving the accused's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

34. Considering the above, it is seen that even if it is established, that the accused had been driving the offending vehicle in question on the day of the incident in question, it is no where proved as to same being driven rashly or negligently, PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 18/22 which is a sine qua non for establishing the guilt of the accused U/s 279 IPC.
35.

sentences.text: All in all therefore, it is seen that there is nothing on record to prove the charges against the accused on the touchstone of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
Prosecution has failed to keep its version intact.
There are gnawing holes at every step which have remain unexplained.

The state version therefore, taken individually and collectively, alongwith the testimonies of its various witnesses, is seen to be grossly incapable in establishing an unbroken chain which could be said to link the accused to the crime as alleged.
In such a scenario, benefit of doubt should definitely be said to have accrued in favour of the accused.
In the result, the accused Surinder Singh is acquitted of offence under Sections 279 of Indian Penal Code.

CHARGE UNDER SECTION 427 IPC 36. Section 427 IPC is reproduced below:
427. Mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees.

--Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to the amount of fifty rupees or upwards,
shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
37. To constitute the offence punishable u/s 427 IPC, the prosecution has to prove the mischief.
The mischief has been defined in Section 425 IPC.

PS- Paharganj State Vs. Surinder Singh page 19/22 Section 425 IPC is also reproduced here.:
State vs Surender Singh on 18 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135723944/
10

"Whoever with intend to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, causes the destruction of any property or any such change in any property or in the situation thereof as destroyed or diminishes its value or utility or affects it injuriously, commits mischief".
38.

To constitute the offence punishable U/s 427 IPC, the prosecution has to prove the following two ingredients:
(i) That there was an intention or knowledge on the part of the accused, committing the offence of mischief that by such act he would cause wrongful loss or damage to some person.
( ii) That the accused has in fact caused the destruction of such property.

39. In the facts of the case before me, though the second ingredient stated above i.e. the accused caused the destruction of the property stands established as the collision between the offending vehicle and the victim's vehicle is an admitted fact and has been otherwise, duly proved by the prosecution.

It is apparent that in order to ascribe criminal liability to the accused, the prosecution bears the onus of proving his reckless conduct and failure to exercise due care.
In the absence of corroborating testimony from individuals who were purportedly present at the scene, the prosecution's case becomes susceptible to questions regarding its accuracy and completeness.
Spot photography serves as crucial visual evidence, documenting the crime scene and aiding in the understanding of the sequence of events.
It assists in establishing the condition of the vehicles involved, the positioning of the vehicles, and any other relevant physical evidence.
The absence of spot photography raises concerns about the thoroughness and integrity of the investigation, thereby weakening the prosecution's case.
This omission is particularly significant in cases of road accidents, where the precise positioning of vehicles, skid marks, and other physical evidence can contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the incident.
The lack of photographic evidence compromises the court's ability to objectively assess the circumstances and make an informed judgment.
Undoubtedly, this lapse diminishes the strength and substance of the prosecution's case.
Moreover,
it is imperative to note that the mechanical inspection reports pertaining to the vehicles implicated in the purported incident, merely produce a concise account of the damages sustained by the said vehicles, without delving into the underlying factors that may have caused such damages.
Moreover, there exist significant and material contradictions within the prosecution's case that cast doubt upon the integrity of the investigative process.
Such lapses on part of the IO in vehicular accident cases leave a yawning gap qua proving the case in a court of law, exactly what has happened in the instant case at hand as well.
Even the site plan filed on record, does not show the respective positioning of the vehicles at the time of alleged incident.
It also fails to specify the exact place of incident as the 'Mark A' as referred as the place of accident, is missing in the site plan.
As such,
therefore, the same are found to be not entirely reliable.

The conflicting narratives put forth by both the accused and the complainant further exacerbate the situation.
Both parties accuse each other of negligence, which necessitates a thorough examination of the evidence and an assessment of the credibility of their claims.
In the absence of concrete evidence and reliable witnesses, it becomes arduous to ascertain the actual cause of the accident and apportion blame solely on the accused.
In light of the foregoing, it is incumbent upon the court to ensure that the prosecution discharges its burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
In the present case, the prosecution has failed to provide substantial evidence to establish the guilt of the accused.
The absence of public witnesses, the failure to conduct spot photography, the lack of suitable crime scene documentation, and the absence of independent witnesses all combine to create reasonable doubt.
The state version therefore, taken individually and collectively, alongwith the testimonies of its various witnesses, is seen to be grossly incapable in establishing an unbroken chain which could be said to link the accused to the crime as alleged.
